Forced to move in a mass, they fell against one another and trampled one another down. Some were killed at once among the spears and equipment; others, tangled in it, were swept downstream. The Syracusans took positions on the far bank --which was steep--and shot down at the Athenians from above. Most of the Athenians drank eagerly, jostling one another in the hollow of the riverbed. The Peloponnesians came down after them and slaughtered chiefly those in the river. The water was soon fouled, but even so they drank it, muddied and bloodied; many fought over it. That is, so desperate was the plight of the routed Athenian army -- once an empire the envy of the Mediterranean world -- that its humiliated soldiers spent their dying moments slurping the blood of fallen comrades without thought of the murder raining down upon their heads. Now... at the risk of sounding overly dramatic, the reason this passage comes to mind is because of the result of the elections. You need not have read much Thucydides to understand which political party is lying in puddles of blood and mire, electorally speaking. Sign up for The Robinson Report. It's free! On the national front, it seems plain to me that President Donald Trump's decision to launch a war of choice against Iran on behalf of Israel while the vast majority of Americans were primarily concerned with affording food and housing was the proximate cause of the landslide. If Trump had focused on doing the things that he said he was going to do during his campaign, as opposed to doing things that he campaigned against, the Republicans might have lost some races, but the damage would not have been so severe. Broadly speaking, these election results are what happens when millions of conservatives and independents decide that perhaps voting isn't really worth it. | | ---|---|--- Maine, in some ways, bucked the national trend. Now, this map could be the result of the tens of millions of dollars that flowed into the state on behalf of Susan Collins, but I'm choosing for the sake of my own self-esteem to believe that Maine's an outlier here because it's the only state with The Maine Wire conducting aggressive investigative reporting. That being said... the Maine GOP has been, once again, humiliated into despair. As I write this, tens of thousands of lifelong Mainers -- Old Mainers, you might call them, irrespective of their age -- are eyeing the exits. Florida? New Hampshire? Tennessee? Is there somewhere you can run to where the schools won't be run for the benefit of corrupt teachers unions and transgender radicals? Is there another state that won't steal your money to enrich the friends and family of politicians, while simultaneously protecting organized crime and racketeering operations? Are there places where the cities aren't overrun with fentanyl-brained zombies, scaggy-armed with taxpayer-subsidized syringes, leaking their HIV-positive blood all over the children's playground? Those who've placed Donald Trump at the center of their existence and allowed their hatred of him to animate their every impulse can be happy for a moment. But their lives aren't really going to change, except for perhaps they'll need something new to replenish their hatred in a few years. I'm sure J.D. Vance and Marco Rubio are up for the task. But for those who haven't been hanging out on overpasses wagging foreign flags, the question over every dinner table is whether Maine has crossed the socialist event horizon. That is, has Maine veered so close to the sucking black-hole maw of centrally planned corruption that there will be no reversing the economic, demographic, and cultural decline. The answer to that question will depend, in large part, on the beleaguered conservative movement, if you can call it a movement. Those of the conservative disposition find themselves, once again, confused and leaderless, relegated to super minority status, destined to be ruled by DSA Democrats from the failed cities of Portland, Lewiston, and Bangor. We conservatives are like the Athenians, drowning in blood and mire, except we never even had a fond empire to remember, apart from the good ole days when Maine actually had an economy that wasn't wholly dependent on government spending and political patronage. Whether the conservative movement can coalesce into a viable insurgency will become apparent over the next few weeks. Today, Republican senators and Republican House members will select leaders from their diminished ranks. Similarly, the chairman of the Maine Republican Party will appoint members of a nominating committee on Nov. 15, the beginning of the process that will determine whether current Maine GOP Chairman Jim Deyermond gets another two-year term. That party election will come in January, around the time the 133rd State Legislature is convening. As the conservatives of Maine begin to navigate the next two years, it's worth looking back at the unlearned lessons of the past. To return to Thucydides: It will be enough for me, however, if these words of mine are judged useful by those who want to understand clearly the events which happened in the past and which (human nature being what it is) will, at some time or other and in much the same ways, be repeated in the future. In other words, Thucydides wrote and studied history primarily because human nature's immutability means that past events offer a preview into future events. What happened before is a guide to what will happen in the future. So with that as a starting point, we must begin by asking: What has happened within the Maine Republican Party that has produced such a miserable record of failure? How did Maine Republicans get wiped out by a party that has, over the last eight years, made life worse for Mainers by every conceivable metric? The origin of our current predicament could be found in any of the post-LePage years. But I place it in the Covid-19 period, when the Republican Party ceded all manner of authority -- executive, moral, legal -- to Gov. Janet Mills. With all prudence cast aside, and federal Biden Bucks raining on Maine, Mills was able to buy off every pet constituency. That includes the no-bid contracts she used to secretly construct a political machine that would greatly aid in her re-election in 2022, as I've detailed at length with our reporting on Gateway Community Services. As some of you may recall, in 2022, the consultants and campaign managers and analysts (all of whom make far more money than anyone at the Maine Wire) were predicting a "Red Wave." Commentator Phil Harriman predicted a full sweep for the red team, with 81 seats in the House, while then-BDN columnist and Maine Policy Institute CEO Matt Gagnon offered a slightly more measured view that there was a chance to flip the Senate. The nominal leaders of the Maine Republican Party were scheming and jockeying for who might become the Speaker of the House or the President of the Senate before the ballots had even been cast. I'm sure I was just as bullish -- or naive -- about the red wave, but I had the wisdom (or cowardice) not to write down any predictions. Wrapped in the mirage that "she kept us safe," Mills defeated ex-Gov-now-Congressman Paul LePage -- both because LePage never directly assailed her totalitarian and unscientific pandemic policies and because he failed to articulate a sound abortion stance. Mills's second term, combined with an NGO complex constructed entirely on taxpayer money, made a formidable coalition. From 2020 to 2024, and perhaps still today, the gay race communists successfully harassed all good men and women out of politics with threats to ruin their lives or businesses for espousing crazy ideas like, maybe high school girls should not be forced to compete athletically against males who say they girls. So just as the Democratic machine was solidifying its formal political power, leftist cultural aggression sent conservatives into retreat. Of course, 2022 was the first of several dismal performances for professional Republicans. The red wave was actually a red humiliation, with GOP candidates shellacked back into minority status here in Maine. Having just taken over TheMaineWire.com, I offered some candid observations about what I'd seen in the lead-up to the unexpected defenestration of the would-be Republican kings who were still measuring leadership office drapes by the time the polls started dousing them in reality. You can go back to the post-mortem I wrote in 2022 following that disastrous election. In that controversial piece of writing, I correctly predicted what Maine was about to experience over the next four years. [Gov. Janet] Mills could reverse course on her campaign promises, hike the income tax to 10 percent, encircle Swan's Island with offshore windmills, legalize fourth trimester abortion, and put a Planned Parenthood in every county, and I'm not sure Republicans in Augusta would be able to win majorities two years from now. In fact, Gov. Mills and the Democratic majorities did raise our taxes, they did protect costly green energy scams, and they did impose the most extreme late-term infanticide law in Western Civilization. They imposed harsh gun control, expanded gender ideology into virtually every public space, and created an express superhighway for noncitizens to get welfare vis-a-vis the "Office of New Americans." Welfare fraud exploded almost exponentially while Asian transnational organized crime ran riot through rural Maine. Taxes soared and spending soared even more, leaving the Democrat coalition of the 133rd Legislature with a more than $1 billion deficit, which they will invariably tackle by hiking taxes even more on the handful of productive working people who've yet to escape this state. My Jeremiah-like warnings fell on deaf ears. Here's the important point from four years ago that went ignored: The dwindling few Republicans who will inhabit the State House this next legislative session need a clean slate. Otherwise, they might as well spare taxpayers the per diem and stay at home. Anyone remotely connected to the old leadership must step back and allow a new generation of conservatives to lead the party. This includes staffers in the House and Senate GOP offices... I know the talent pool for Republican operatives is shallow in Maine, but we're at rock bottom here... As for new leadership, placing young, media savvy, strategically minded conservatives in charge is the only possible path to becoming relevant again... None of this was particularly insightful or brilliant. After a professional football team goes multiple seasons without a single win, they typically change up the coach, the quarterback, and the strategy. But Republican leaders -- whoever those are or were -- did nothing of the sort. No new staff was hired. No new leaders were elevated. No new ideas or tactics were deployed. The same tired hands wrote the same tired scripts to blather out on the same AM radio signals to the same tired audience. Throughout the next legislative sessions, Republicans plowed through with the same perma-minority mindset that believes, falsely, that the extreme leftists who wear the Democrat name tags are interested in good-faith negotiations over policies that will improve the lives of Mainers. (Pro tip: They aren't.) These leftist extremists who operate under the banner of the Maine Democratic Party are only interested in power, control, and money, with maybe a few naive youngsters still stupid enough to believe that "social justice" was ever a real thing. They will lie, cheat, and steal to get more power, control, and money, and you cannot negotiate in good faith with Democratic politicians and radicalized DSA staffers who will lie, cheat, and steal to advance their narrow, selfish interests. Yet, like Charlie Brown with the football, Republicans plodded ahead in the last three legislative sessions again and again for a kick, only to cry about sore asses on the House floor with speeches no one listens to and no one cares about. Meanwhile, Lucy snickers with her friends, counting stacks of cash, and chortling about stupid and gullible the conservatives. That's not the only prescient wisdom I dispensed four years ago. Here's another bit: If a Republican donor wanted to make a substantial difference in future state elections, he should consider making a large donation only on the condition that it be used to construct an elite early voting and mail-in voting apparatus. Voting in modern elections now takes place over several weeks. Conservatives may not like it, it may open the door for fraud and bureaucratic shenanigans, but it's a reality. These are the rules and this is the playing field. If Republicans want to win, they must show up early, not just on game day. Whether a GOP mega donor stepped up to the plate to fund such an effort, I don't know. Judging by the chronic indebtedness of the Maine Republican Party, I'm guessing no. Also: the results are right there in the early voting numbers. From 2022 to 2026, Republicans were clobbered in the early voting contest, even though they did make some slight progress in closing the gap. In 2022, Democrats had 64,622 more early voters than the Republicans did, a lead that dropped to 41,488 in 2026. However, Republicans managed to have 60,174 absentee ballot requests four years ago but just 31,618 this year. Very obviously, no concerted effort has been made to level the playing field in early voting. Trump bears most blame for this. His imbecilic pooh-poohing of early voting was a generational mistake. But he's not the only Republican with a platform. Who knows where the GOP might be sitting if they'd embraced some early voting initiatives, as conservative groups in other states have done so successfully. Indeed, if Republicans had embraced early voting with any kind of success, Democrats like Shenna Bellows might be out there condemning early voting as undemocratic! Four years after my unheeded call for a better early voting program, I would also recommend that Maine conservatives embrace large-language models as a tool to help them fight from a minority and poorly financed position. Used properly, new and emerging technology could be the equivalent of giving the Mujahideen shoulder-fired rockets to take on the vastly superior Soviet forces. Of course, this would require them to listen to my earlier advice about hiring some staff who weren't already collecting Social Security when the Soviet Union was mucking around in Afghanistan. In case I haven't made myself clear, the GOP caucuses in the State House need to utterly gut the current staffer ranks and consultant ranks and come up with some brand new talent if they want anything to change. If they continue to pay the same staff and the same consultants, they will continue to get the same results. This Substack is reader-supported. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. The other area where the Maine Republican Party has seriously disadvantaged itself and must reform if it wishes to alter the trajectory of the state is structural and financial. Briefly, the Maine GOP's approach to raising and spending money is scattered and non-strategic. Compounding the problem, Republicans in Maine have a reputation among the donor class for being a group of greedy over-promisers who will both steal your money and lose. Word spreads fast among GOP donors. One untrustworthy consultant or politician can create a negative feedback loop that leads to even good or worthy causes being ignored because of the perception that conservatives in Maine are not to be trusted. Earning back that trust will require a radical reformation of how the party operates. Before explaining the money game at play in state politics, it's useful to understand a few things about how state legislative races are funded. Whether you like it or not, political campaigns require communicating ideas, and communicating ideas typically requires money. For both political parties, there are three principal political committees that endure regardless of individual personalities. These are used to raise money for the party state committees and legislative caucuses. On each side, there's the state committee, the state senate caucus committee, and the state house committee. Yes, there are dozens of other interest group funds and leadership PACs, but those are of less importance to this discussion than the big three central committees that set tone and strategy for party operations. The most obvious fact that emerges from a cursory review of campaign finance documents is that the Maine Democratic Party and the Maine Republican Party are operated and governed according to completely different rules, philosophies, and strategies. The election results are the supreme judge of which party has the more effective mode of operation. Demonstrably, the Maine Democrats are running a more successful fundraising operation than the Republicans (which typically happens when a party can actually deliver legislation for pharmaceutical lobbies and other corporate interests), but the left-wing party is also much better at managing and deploying that cash to earn votes. On the Democratic side, the House and Senate committees engage in regular fundraising. They wine and dine lobbyists, hold special events, and do the routine business of raising campaign cash. The expenditures are typically limited to the cost of fundraising: mail, payroll, office equipment, food and rent. But the key part is that eventually, a big chunk of the money raised by that committee is transferred to the central Democratic State Committee. The same goes for the Democratic Senate Committee. Regardless of who is running either political committee, the expenses are lean and all of the money flows to the central committee. From 2018 through the available 2026 filings, the Democratic Senate and House committees reported payments to the state party of $10.51 million and $5.22 million, respectively, compared with $1.46 million and $216,640 from their Republican counterparts. The Democrats' current charter puts finances under a Finance Subcommittee and the annual budget before the Democratic State Committee. It also establishes a coordinated campaign committee for voter identification, absentee ballots, turnout, and voter files. Once the money hits the central committee, the decisions about how to allocate that money are not made by a single chairman or executive director. Instead, the Democratic Party is governed by a committee so that many sets of hands and eyes have oversight over how campaign cash is being distributed. That's important for a few reasons. For one, it ensures that a shared and overarching strategic vision is overseeing the allocation of resources. That makes it less likely that a vulnerable incumbent will not get support or a candidate with a comfortable lead will get resources that could be spent elsewhere. Equally importantly, committee decision making over the allocation of resources ensures that campaign contributions are not steered for the benefit of narrow financial interests. The spending mix is different, too. The campaign finance reports show Democrats reported $4.46 million for mailers and printed literature against Republicans' $1.47 million, and $4.65 million for payroll and staff against $1.41 million. Republicans reported $9.29 million for television and cable against Democrats' $1.93 million. That is a stark difference in what the committees bought. Of course, there's some overlap between the state campaign finance filings and the federal campaign finance filings, so these numbers aren't exactly perfect. But the records suffice to show significant differences in how the two parties raise, manage, and deploy resources. The clearest way the Maine GOP could reform its various fundraising organs is by establishing governance via committee so that narrow interests can't dominate campaign spending in ways that are guided by something other than winning. Because let's face it: politics is a nasty game. It's even nastier behind the curtain with the consultants living that feast-or-famine lifestyle, hustling from election to election. Then you add to that the skim. For those who don't know, politics is filled with people who make money by skimming. They skim the fundraising. They skim the junk mail that clutters your mailbox and goes right in the garbage. They skim the television ads and the radio ads and the social media ads. A politician hires a fundraising consultant who helps him raise $500,000 for his campaign? Well, the fundraising consultant gets a slice of that treasure chest, even if all he did was provide a Rolodex and some talking points. Now, say that politician wants to spend $250,000 on television ads. Somewhere in the middle a political consultant is getting a skim -- could be 15%, 20%, or even more. Who's keeping track of that skim? Usually the one doing the skimming. But that's how political campaigns raise campaign cash and transform it into communications that reach voters. There's nothing inherently wrong with the skim -- everyone has to eat -- but it does create perverse incentives to deploy resources in ways that prioritize something other than winning. For example, if you're getting the TV skim, you're probably going to recommend lots of TV. Ditto if you're getting the mail skim. If it turns out that paying young activists to door knock is the more effective strategy, but you're not getting a skim on the door-knocking... well, the door-knocking might get pushed to the back burner. Whoever emerges as the next crop of Republican leaders needs to take a careful look at who had been skimming and whether that skimming has been oriented toward the good of the party or toward narrower interests. Even if winning has been the top priority, a party that purports to back meritocracy ought to find a way to swiftly replace professionals with demonstrated losing records. The last thing I'll say, at the risk of sounding too harsh on Maine's Republicans, considering that they're still drowning in their own blood and mire while spears and arrows rain down on their heads, is that they are vastly outmatched not only by a better funded and better run Democratic Party, but also by a humongous leftist dark-money operation that works hand-in-glove with official Democrats to advance the same goals, often in more vicious ways. I'm talking, of course, about the constellation of 501(c)3 and 501(c)4 and other NGOs funded by George Soros, Hansjorg Wyss, Pierre Omidyar, and many other leftist billionaires. Unlike the Maine Republicans, the Maine Democrats have both the Bangor and Portland newspapers effectively serving as their communications and propaganda organs. And they have dozens and dozens of NGOs that get both dark-money funding and taxpayer dollars. The playing field is tilted and the game is unfair. Conservatives can either whine about it, get better at politics, or move to New Hampshire. | | | | * ---|---|--- | Nov 4 | You 're receiving The Robinson Report for free. Our movement accomplished something unimaginable on Tuesday night. **Well, not to me.**
My team and I entered this fight knowing we were on the cusp of making history, so we held nothing back. We scoured the nation for fearless climate leaders, and as of this morning, **we’ve elected 216 this year.**
In my decades of activism, I have always believed in one simple truth: everyday people have the power to create change when we come together. **Now, together, we have fundamentally shifted what power looks like in this country.**
Thank you for making this possible.
I want you to see what our climate champions ran on:
_Holding Big Tech Accountable._
_Stopping AI data center expansion._
_Passing polluter pay legislation._
_Lowering utility bills for everyday people._
**This message is loud and clear. And our candidates overcame enormous odds to deliver it.**
Corporate polluters and outside groups bankrolled by Donald Trump’s super PAC and Elon Musk poured hundreds of millions to try to buy this election.
They had bottomless bank accounts, but we had something much stronger: a people-powered movement that cared too much to sit this one out.
This election was a test of whose interests our government serves.
By showing up, knocking on doors, and chipping in what you could, you sent an unmistakable reminder that climate is in fact a winning message. These issues are on the forefront of our minds, and they need to be a priority for our elected officials.
Thank you, thank you, thank you for trusting us. I do not take your support for granted. Onward!
xx Jane

Looking back. Looking Forward

| | | [ ](https://home.forwardparty.com/r?u=MtBLw57MCBnd28lIl741uxhE24SlqUGA-DgV4-cYEvs&e=61868e7acdd36ae0ddf3e39aa8429171&utm_source=forwardparty&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=2026_november_newsletter&n=1)
---
---
### Over the Shoulder, Over the Horizon
Elections have consequences, but also, elections sometimes are the consequences. The Republicans are seeing the consequence of allowing Trump to govern the way he has for the past two years. We'll see if the Democrats have learned what happens when the leadership keeps out new voices. How do either of them explain the rise in Americans calling themselves Independent? The Major Parties have a lot to learn, but maybe we do too. We've been building this Party for nearly 5 years. Are we on the right track? How have things changed in that time? What have we learned? What should be our goals for the next 5 years? How do we accomplish them? Many of you have emailed us over the past 5 years with ideas or comments about what you'd like to see. While we all are understanding the blue wave that hit our State this week, before we start planning for 2027, let's consider the big picture. Please share your thoughts on these questions or what ever you're thinking. You can reply to this email or share on our SLACK channel. If you haven't joined already, use the link below. **You are a Forwardist. Help us understand what that means to you.**
---
[ ](https://home.forwardparty.com/r?u=OO1xB82Dwc0SwW5xslNAt5demYUjnvMsNObg_2SsnH4C04dQQgB9BZ02TA7y9H7t-4vbxkv79HHUmZ6qj3hodVNslc1j8BmCJ3lol1yOotH-UbK54WKgqDyUAWXEaQfXHk95ddnmDRn_oLR7jfB_Sg&e=61868e7acdd36ae0ddf3e39aa8429171&utm_source=forwardparty&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=2026_november_newsletter&n=2)
---
* * *
---
### Volunteer with PA Forward Party
2027 is a year for building local engagement and local campaigns. We plan to hold more events and get our message out to a wider audience. We want to define our goals clearly to that audience. We want to find new ways to support the candidates who affiliate with us and recruit more great candidates in the future. If you want to help, this is the time to get involved.

---
* * *
---
## 2026 Candidates!
We want to to thank all of our 2026 Forward endorsed candidates. Election night was very exciting watching all the returns come in and there were a lot of close races. These races didn't ultimately go the way we hoped but we're proud of the relationships we made and everyone's hard work over the past year. Thanks to those of you who knocked on doors, gathered signatures, made calls, sent texts, or spread the word to help PA Forwardists running for office. This year, we endorsed 2 Republicans, 2 Democrats, and 2 Independents. We're proud to be an organization that can stratal the partisan divide. While our focus will continue to be local and state elections, we had the opportunity this year to work with 2 congressional candidates including the current most bi-partisan member of congress. The 4 State House candidates we endorsed were spread across the state and ran great campaigns. The effort and commitment that goes into one of these campaigns make us endlessly grateful that these candidates would throw their hat in the ring.
